title: Idioms & phrases
examples: What does 'break a leg' actually mean?
Can you give me an example of an idiom I can use today?
How is an idiom different from a regular phrase?

explain.say: Today we are learning about idioms and phrases. An idiom has a special meaning. It does not mean what the words say.

items: An idiom has a hidden meaning.

explain.say: For example, if we say something is 'a piece of cake'. This does not mean it is actually food. It means it is very easy to do.
Another common idiom is 'bite the bullet'. This means to face a difficult situation. You must do it even if it is hard.
We must also learn about usage. Using an idiom correctly makes your speaking sound natural. It helps you speak like a native speaker.
Imagine you are talking about a test you found simple. You could say it was 'a piece of cake'. This shows good usage.

draw.text: Test was a piece of cake.

explain.say: A common mistake is taking idioms literally. If you say 'spill the beans', you should not look for actual beans. It means to reveal a secret.

faq.q: What is the difference between an idiom and a phrase?
faq.a: A phrase is a group of words that work together grammatically. An idiom is a phrase whose meaning is completely different from the words themselves.

faq.q: Can I use idioms in my writing?
faq.a: Yes, you can use them in your writing to make it more colourful. However, always make sure the reader knows the meaning.
asks: Is it okay to use idioms in essays?
Should I use idioms all the time?

faq.q: How do I learn more idioms?
faq.a: The best way is to read books and watch movies. When you hear an idiom, try to guess its meaning first.
asks: Where can I find more idioms?
What is the best way to learn them?

faq.a: Yes, every idiom has a specific, understood meaning within English. If it doesn't have a common meaning, it might not be an idiom.
asks: What if the meaning is unclear?

faq.a: Learning them helps you speak more fluently and sound more natural. It is a key part of advanced English speaking.
asks: Is learning idioms important for speaking?
Will I sound better if I know idioms?

facts: Idioms are phrases whose collective meaning cannot be guessed from the individual words.
Knowing idioms helps improve speaking fluency and vocabulary range.
Learning an idiom requires understanding its figurative meaning, not its literal meaning.
Common idioms often relate to everyday actions or feelings.

quiz.say: If someone says you passed the test like 'a piece of cake', what do they mean?
quiz.why: This means the task required little effort, which is the common meaning of the idiom.

wrong.0: This changes the subject entirely and does not relate to the difficulty of the test.
wrong.2: This is the literal meaning of the words, but idioms have a different, non-literal meaning.
wrong.3: This focuses only on the word 'piece' and ignores the idiomatic context.

quiz.say: What does the idiom 'bite the bullet' suggest you must do?
quiz.why: This idiom means accepting something unpleasant because it must be done, showing courage.

wrong.0: This is the literal action described by the words, ignoring the figurative meaning.
wrong.1: This focuses only on the word 'bite' and misses the context of difficulty.
wrong.2: This misunderstands the object 'bullet' as something related to guns.

quiz.say: If you reveal a secret, which idiom fits best?
quiz.why: This idiom specifically means to accidentally or intentionally reveal secret information.

wrong.1: This is not a recognized idiom and does not convey the same sense of revelation.
wrong.2: This is too literal and does not match the established idiomatic phrase.
wrong.3: While it means telling the truth, it is not the standard idiomatic expression.
